Um, high? Like, full of energy? No. Definitely not. I mean, like I was trying to explain earlier, my battery is just totally empty, so having too much energy is pretty much the exact opposite of what I experience. I don't think I've ever had a time where I felt like I had extra energy to burn. I never had days where I was bouncing off the walls or feeling like I could take on the world or anything like that. 

And irritable... I mean, my mom gets frustrated with me, like I mentioned, when she stands in my doorway and asks me questions over and over, but I don't get mad at her. I don't snap at her or feel irritable at all. I just sit there. Because, if you think about it, anger or irritability is a really active feeling, you know? You have to have fuel to burn to be mad, your heart has to race and you have to want to push back, and I just don't have any fuel for that. It takes way too much effort to be angry. 

It's funny, because sometimes I actually think my mom almost wishes I would get mad, or get super energetic, just so I'd be doing something, literally anything other than just staring at the carpet in the same clothes. Like, if I suddenly jumped up and decided to clean the whole house or knit ten scarves in a row, she'd probably be thrilled, but that's just never happened. I've never had four days like that. I don't think I've even had four minutes like that. So, no, definitely no extra energy or feeling high.

Um... two years? Yeah. Actually, it's been a little longer than that. This whole decline, or whatever you want to call it, has been going on since I started the community-college program. That was about two years and two months ago. 

I know the exact timeline because it was the fall right after I graduated high school, and my mom was so excited for me to start taking classes. So, yeah, it’s been going on most days—really, pretty much every single day—since that semester started two years and two months ago. The days just sort of blur together into one long, flat line since then, because when you're just existing, a Tuesday feels exactly the same as a Saturday. My mom still hasn't taken that printed schedule off my door, actually. I look at it sometimes when I'm sitting there. So it's definitely been over two years of this.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Um, no, I haven't. I mean, I know you just asked about feeling depressed or down, and I guess this is kind of the same thing, but for two weeks? No. Not even for two weeks. Like I was saying, there's just no water to drown in. It's not like I have this baseline of being flat and then suddenly, for a couple of weeks, I dip down into this really dark, heavy depression where I can't function because I'm so sad. 

My functioning is already... well, it's already what it is. I sit in my room. I look at the carpet. But it's not because I'm overwhelmed by sadness or despair. It's just the emptiness. I don't have these episodes where the flatness suddenly turns into some intense, agonizing depression that stops me from doing things. The flatness is what stops me from doing things. 

I remember reading once, back when I used to read things for that English class I never finished, about how depression can make people feel like they're walking through molasses, you know? Like everything is thick and heavy and takes so much effort just to push through. But for me, it's not like walking through molasses. It's like... not walking at all. It's like the concept of walking just doesn't even apply anymore. There's no struggle against a heavy feeling, there's just an absence of the drive to move. 

So, no, I haven't had any two-week periods where I felt so depressed it interfered with my functioning. My functioning has been exactly the same—just sitting there, staring at the floor, listening to the hum of the refrigerator from the kitchen—every day for the last two years and two months. There hasn't been any dip into sadness or anything like that. Just the same flat line, day after day, week after week.

Um... lost my appetite? No. No, I haven't. I mean, it's just like the other things we were talking about. It's not like I get excited about food, but I haven't lost my appetite, not for two weeks or even a few days. 

My mom, she brings me meals on this little wooden tray. It has these handles cut into the sides, and the varnish is kind of wearing off on the left corner where she always grips it. She brings it in three times a day, like clockwork. Sometimes she makes those little frozen pizza rolls, or sometimes it's just a turkey sandwich, and she actually cuts the crusts off now, which she hasn't done since I was maybe seven years old. I'll take a bite of the sandwich, and I'll chew it, and I'll swallow it, and then I'll take a sip of water from the blue plastic cup she always brings. It's just mechanics, you know? Like putting gas in a car that's just sitting in the driveway and never going anywhere. 

Sometimes I'll sit there for an hour, just holding a piece of bread, looking at the way the crust is slightly darker on one side, feeling the soft texture of it between my fingers before I take the next bite. I can feel the crumbs falling onto the blanket. But I always finish it. It doesn't really taste like much anymore—not good, not bad, just texture and chewing. But my stomach still growls if she's late bringing the tray. Like, if she goes to the grocery store and lunch is at two instead of noon, my stomach makes noises. My body still knows it needs food, even if my brain doesn't really care about eating. 

So, no, there hasn't been any time where I stopped eating or lost my appetite like that. I just eat the food she brings in the exact same flat way I do everything else. I just sit there, and I chew, and I watch the crumbs fall.

I try to tell her I'm not crying, but she just looks at me like I'm hiding it. But I'm really not.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?\n\nPatient: Um... I don't know if \"lost interest\" is really the right way to describe it. Because it's not like I suddenly hate knitting or think it's stupid now. I still have this one really soft, chunky blue yarn sitting right on my nightstand, it's the kind of yarn that's really thick and warm, and I know I like it. I know it's a good color, I picked it out specifically at the craft store a while ago. And my journal, it has this nice leather cover with a little strap, and I know I usually like writing in it with this specific black gel pen because the ink glides really smoothly over the paper... I know those are things I enjoy. Or, well, things I know are enjoyable. \n\nBut when I look at them now, I don't have this thought of, 'ugh, I don't care about this anymore' or 'this is pointless.' I just... don't feel the spark to reach out and grab them. It's not a loss of liking it, it's just... I don't know. Like with the snacks my mom brings. She brought me those little cheddar cheese crackers yesterday, the ones shaped like little squares that I've eaten since I was like, seven years old. I know they taste good. I know I like them. But I just let the bowl sit there on the blanket next to me until they got stale because the whole process of picking one up, chewing it, tasting it... it just didn't happen. \n\nSo I don't think I lost interest, not really. The interest is still there in the room, I guess, I just can't connect to it. Does that make sense? Because my mom keeps saying I must hate my hobbies now since I won't touch them, and I have to keep explaining to her—well, in my head I explain it, because like I said, talking takes too much energy—that I don't hate them, I'm just sitting there instead.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least four days when you felt unusually high, irritable, or full of energy?\n\nPatient: Um, high? Like, full of energy? No. Definitely not. I mean, like I was trying to explain earlier, my battery is just totally empty, so having too much energy is pretty much the exact opposite of what I experience. I don't think I've ever had a time where I felt like I had extra energy to burn. Even back in high school, before I just started sitting in my room all the time, I was always just kind of a normal, quiet person. I never had days where I was bouncing off the walls or feeling like I could take on the world or anything like that. \n\nAnd irritable... I mean, my mom gets frustrated with me, like I mentioned, when she stands in my doorway and asks me questions over and over, but I don't get mad at her. I don't snap at her or feel irritable at all. I just sit there. Because, if you think about it, anger or irritability is a really active feeling, you know? You have to have fuel to burn to be mad, your heart has to race and you have to want to push back, and I just don't have any fuel for that. It takes way too much effort to be angry. \n\nIt's funny, because sometimes I actually think my mom almost wishes I would get mad, or get super energetic, just so I'd be doing something, literally anything other than just staring at the carpet in the same clothes. Like, if I suddenly jumped up and decided to clean the whole house or knit ten scarves in a row, she'd probably be thrilled, but that's just never happened. I've never had four days like that. I don't think I've even had four minutes like that. Actually, it's been a little longer than that. This whole decline, or whatever you want to call it, has been going on since I started the community-college program. That was about two years and two months ago. \n\nI know the exact timeline because it was the fall right after I graduated high school, and my mom was so excited for me to start taking classes. We went to the campus bookstore together and got my textbooks, and we bought these color-coded folders, and I had this whole class schedule printed out and taped to the back of my bedroom door. I was supposed to take an intro to history class and some English composition class, I think. But... I only went for maybe a week or two before this whole flat feeling just really took over completely. \n\nI remember sitting in the lecture hall for history and just staring at the back of the plastic chair in front of me, just kind of tracing the little scratches in the plastic with my eyes, and realizing I just didn't have the energy to lift my pen or even process what the professor was saying. I started staying in my room, just sitting on the edge of the bed looking at the carpet, exactly like I do now. \n\nSo, yeah, it’s been going on most days—really, pretty much every single day—since that semester started two years and two months ago. My mom still hasn't taken that printed schedule off my door, actually. I look at it sometimes when I'm sitting there. It's just hanging there, curling at the bottom edges where the tape is giving out, but I don't have the energy to peel it off, and I guess she doesn't want to either. So it's definitely been over two years of this.\n\nDoctor: Even though you’ve said you don’t feel sad, have there been times over these past two years when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Um... depressed or down? Like, if you're depressed, I imagine you feel heavy or sad or you cry, or you have these dark thoughts circling in your head. But I don't have any of that. It's just... blank. Are you just so depressed you can't move?\" And I remember looking at her and trying to find some sadness in myself to match hers, because she was so upset, but there was just nothing there. Like I was saying, there's just no water to drown in. It's not like I have this baseline of being flat and then suddenly, for a couple of weeks, I dip down into this really dark, heavy depression where I can't function because I'm so sad. \n\nMy functioning is already... well, it's already what it is. I sit in my room. I look at the carpet. But it's not because I'm overwhelmed by sadness or despair. It's just the emptiness. I don't have these episodes where the flatness suddenly turns into some intense, agonizing depression that stops me from doing things. The flatness is what stops me from doing things. \n\nI remember reading once, back when I used to read things for that English class I never finished, about how depression can make people feel like they're walking through molasses, you know? Like everything is thick and heavy and takes so much effort just to push through. But for me, it's not like walking through molasses. It's like... not walking at all. It's like the concept of walking just doesn't even apply anymore. There's no struggle against a heavy feeling, there's just an absence of the drive to move. \n\nSo, no, I haven't had any two-week periods where I felt so depressed it interfered with my functioning. My functioning has been exactly the same—just sitting there, staring at the floor, listening to the hum of the refrigerator from the kitchen—every day for the last two years and two months. There hasn't been any dip into sadness or anything like that. Just the same flat line, day after day, week after week.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any period of at least two weeks when you felt clearly depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Um, no. I mean, I know you're asking about the two weeks thing again, but it's really just exactly like I was saying before. There hasn't been a time where I felt depressed or down like that. Not for two weeks, not for two days. It's just... I think people really struggle to understand that you can be completely non-functional without being sad. \n\nLike, my mom, she's always trying to find a reason for it. She'll come into my room and she'll open the curtains, the ones with the little blue flowers on them that we picked out when I was in middle school, and she'll say, \"Let some light in, maybe it'll lift your mood.\" And the light comes in, and it hits the carpet, and I can see all the little dust motes floating in the sunbeam, just drifting around in the air. I can watch them for hours, just seeing how they catch the light and then disappear into the shadows near the closet door. But watching them doesn't make me feel better, and it doesn't make me feel worse. It just... is. \n\nI don't have a mood to lift. That's the thing. If I was depressed, like really down and sad for two weeks, maybe the sunlight would hurt my eyes, or maybe I'd want to hide under the covers and cry because the world is too bright and I'm too sad. But I don't do that. I just sit there on the edge of the bed and look at the dust motes. I don't feel the urge to cry, I don't feel a heaviness in my chest. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Um, didn't you... I'm pretty sure you just asked me that exact same question a few minutes ago. About the two weeks and feeling depressed most of the day? I know you probably have a list of things you have to ask, or boxes you need to check off on your clipboard, but the answer is still exactly the same as it was before. No. I haven't ever had two weeks like that. 

It's strange, though, how time works when you're just... sitting. Two weeks sounds like a really specific, long amount of time when you say it like that, but for me, two weeks is just fourteen days of watching the ceiling fan. We have this ceiling fan in my bedroom, it has four blades, and one of them is slightly warped. It droops down just a fraction of an inch more than the other three. The blades are wood-paneled on one side and plain white on the other, and my dad installed it white-side down when I was ten because he said it made the ceiling look higher. 

I just lie on the bed and watch it not spinning. I can trace the dust along the edge of the warped blade with my eyes. Sometimes I think about what it would feel like to actually care that it's warped, or to feel sad that fourteen days—or a whole month, or a year—are just slipping by while I look at it. If I were actually depressed, like really down the way you keep asking about, maybe I'd cry about wasting my time or something. People who are depressed feel heavy and miserable about things like that, right? They feel bad about themselves. But I don't feel miserable. I don't feel anything about the fan, or the two weeks, or the fact that it's been over a year since high school ended and I'm just here in this room. 

So, yeah, no. I haven't been depressed or down for two weeks. There's no sadness to it. It's just the flat. Just the warped fan blade, and the quiet, and the flat.

We went to the campus bookstore together and got my textbooks, and we bought these color-coded folders, and I had this whole class schedule printed out and taped to the back of my bedroom door. I was supposed to take an intro to history class and some English composition class, I think. But... I only went for maybe a week or two before this whole flat feeling just really took over completely. \n\nI remember sitting in the lecture hall for history and just staring at the back of the plastic chair in front of me, just kind of tracing the little scratches in the plastic with my eyes, and realizing I just didn't have the energy to lift my pen or even process what the professor was saying. The battery was just gone. And then I just stopped going. I started staying in my room, just sitting on the edge of the bed looking at the carpet, exactly like I do now. \n\nSo, yeah, it’s been going on most days—really, pretty much every single day—since that semester started two years and two months ago. The days just sort of blur together into one long, flat line since then, because when you're just existing, a Tuesday feels exactly the same as a Saturday. My mom still hasn't taken that printed schedule off my door, actually. I look at it sometimes when I'm sitting there. It's just hanging there, curling at the bottom edges where the tape is giving out, but I don't have the energy to peel it off, and I guess she doesn't want to either. So it's definitely been over two years of this.\n\nDoctor: Even though you’ve said you don’t feel sad, have there been times over these past two years when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Um... depressed or down? No, not really. Because, like I was trying to explain with the hobbies and the energy, feeling down still feels like it requires some kind of emotional weight, you know? Like, if you're depressed, I imagine you feel heavy or sad or you cry, or you have these dark thoughts circling in your head. But I don't have any of that. It's just... blank. It's not a heavy feeling, it's just an empty feeling. \n\nI actually remember my mom asking me something similar, maybe a year ago? It was winter, I know because I was wearing this thick gray sweater she bought me, the one with the big buttons down the front, and I was just sitting on my bed staring at the corner of the room where the paint is peeling a little bit. And she came in and sat next to me and she was crying, and she asked, \"Are you so sad, honey? Are you just so depressed you can't move?\" And I remember looking at her and trying to find some sadness in myself to match hers, because she was so upset, but there was just nothing there. I didn't feel like crying. I didn't feel sorrow. I didn't feel anything at all. \n\nSo I told her no, I'm not sad. And I think that almost confused her more. Because people expect that if you're not doing anything, if you're just existing in your room for two years, you must be drowning in this deep, dark depression. But I'm not drowning. It's more like... the water just evaporated. There's no water to drown in. There's no sadness, no feeling down. Just the flat line. So, no, I haven't had times where I felt depressed most of the day, because I don't really feel much of anything most of the day.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when, aside from the flatness, you felt so depressed or down that it seriously interfered with your ability to function?\n\nPatient: Um, no, I haven't. I mean, I know you just asked about feeling depressed or down, and I guess this is kind of the same thing, but for two weeks? No. Not even for two weeks. Like I was saying, there's just no water to drown in. It's not like I have this baseline of being flat and then suddenly, for a couple of weeks, I dip down into this really dark, heavy depression where I can't function because I'm so sad. \n\nMy functioning is already... well, it's already what it is. I sit in my room. I look at the carpet. But it's not because I'm overwhelmed by sadness or despair. It's just the emptiness. I don't have these episodes where the flatness suddenly turns into some intense, agonizing depression that stops me from doing things. The flatness is what stops me from doing things. \n\nI remember reading once, back when I used to read things for that English class I never finished, about how depression can make people feel like they're walking through molasses, you know? Like everything is thick and heavy and takes so much effort just to push through. But for me, it's not like walking through molasses. It's like... not walking at all. It's like the concept of walking just doesn't even apply anymore. There's no struggle against a heavy feeling, there's just an absence of the drive to move. \n\nSo, no, I haven't had any two-week periods where I felt so depressed it interfered with my functioning. My functioning has been exactly the same—just sitting there, staring at the floor, listening to the hum of the refrigerator from the kitchen—every day for the last two years and two months. There hasn't been any dip into sadness or anything like that. Just the same flat line, day after day, week after week.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any period of at least two weeks when you felt clearly depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Um, no. I mean, I know you're asking about the two weeks thing again, but it's really just exactly like I was saying before. There hasn't been a time where I felt depressed or down like that. Not for two weeks, not for two days. It's just... I think people really struggle to understand that you can be completely non-functional without being sad. \n\nLike, my mom, she's always trying to find a reason for it. She'll come into my room and she'll open the curtains, the ones with the little blue flowers on them that we picked out when I was in middle school, and she'll say, \"Let some light in, maybe it'll lift your mood.\" And the light comes in, and it hits the carpet, and I can see all the little dust motes floating in the sunbeam, just drifting around in the air. I can watch them for hours, just seeing how they catch the light and then disappear into the shadows near the closet door. But watching them doesn't make me feel better, and it doesn't make me feel worse. It just... is. \n\nI don't have a mood to lift. That's the thing. If I was depressed, like really down and sad for two weeks, maybe the sunlight would hurt my eyes, or maybe I'd want to hide under the covers and cry because the world is too bright and I'm too sad. But I don't do that. I just sit there on the edge of the bed and look at the dust motes. I don't feel the urge to cry, I don't feel a heaviness in my chest. I just feel the complete absence of anything. \n\nSo, no, there's never been a two-week period of feeling clearly depressed or down. It's always just the flat line. The same flat line since I started that community college program two years and two months ago. Just me, the carpet, the dust motes, and the tape curling on the back of my door. No sadness. Just... blank.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a time that lasted at least two weeks when, in addition to this flat feeling, you also lost your appetite?\n\nPatient: Um... lost my appetite? No. No, I haven't. I mean, it's just like the other things we were talking about. It's not like I get excited about food, but I haven't lost my appetite, not for two weeks or even a few days. \n\nMy mom, she brings me meals on this little wooden tray. It has these handles cut into the sides, and the varnish is kind of wearing off on the left corner where she always grips it. She brings it in three times a day, like clockwork. Sometimes she makes those little frozen pizza rolls, or sometimes it's just a turkey sandwich, and she actually cuts the crusts off now, which she hasn't done since I was maybe seven years old. I think she does it because she thinks I'm fragile now, or maybe she just wants to feel like she's doing something special to take care of me since I don't leave the room. \n\nBut I eat it. I don't look at the tray and feel sick, or think, \"Oh, I can't possibly eat.\" I just take the plate, and I sit on the edge of the bed, and I chew. I'll take a bite of the sandwich, and I'll chew it, and I'll swallow it, and then I'll take a sip of water from the blue plastic cup she always brings. It's just mechanics, you know? Like putting gas in a car that's just sitting in the driveway and never going anywhere. \n\nSometimes I'll sit there for an hour, just holding a piece of bread, looking at the way the crust is slightly darker on one side, feeling the soft texture of it between my fingers before I take the next bite. Um, worthless? Or a failure? No... I don't think so. I mean, to feel like a failure, you have to actually have a goal that you care about failing at, right? You have to feel some kind of disappointment in yourself, or care about what you're supposed to be doing. But I don't have that.

It's in this dark green padded folder with the school crest stamped on it in gold foil, and the gold is actually starting to flake off just a tiny bit on the left edge of the shield. I can see the little specks of gold dust on the wood of the shelf if the light hits it right. Sometimes my mom comes in to take my empty plates, and I see her look at that green folder, and then she looks at me just sitting on the bed. I know she's probably thinking about how I was supposed to be finishing that community college program by now. I just stopped going, you know. I didn't make a big decision to quit, I just stopped getting up to go. 

But when I look at the diploma, or when I think about the college classes I'm not taking, my chest doesn't get tight. I don't feel ashamed. I don't sit here thinking, "Oh, I'm so worthless, I'm a failure because I'm nineteen and I just watch the ceiling fan all day." I just look at the green folder. I look at the little flakes of gold on the wood. I don't feel bad about myself, and I don't feel good about myself either. 

I think a failure would be upset about failing. They would cry, or feel guilty that their mom is bringing them turkey sandwiches with the crusts cut off while they do absolutely nothing. But I don't feel guilty. It's just like the dust motes and the warped fan blade. I just exist in the room. There's no judgment attached to it in my head. I'm not worth less, I'm not worth more. I'm just... here. So, no, I haven't been feeling worthless.

I started staying in my room, just sitting on the edge of the bed looking at the carpet, exactly like I do now. \n\nSo, yeah, it’s been going on most days—really, pretty much every single day—since that semester started two years and two months ago. The days just sort of blur together into one long, flat line since then, because when you're just existing, a Tuesday feels exactly the same as a Saturday. My mom still hasn't taken that printed schedule off my door, actually. I look at it sometimes when I'm sitting there. It's just hanging there, curling at the bottom edges where the tape is giving out, but I don't have the energy to peel it off, and I guess she doesn't want to either. So it's definitely been over two years of this.\n\nDoctor: Even though you’ve said you don’t feel sad, have there been times over these past two years when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Um... depressed or down? No, not really. Because, like I was trying to explain with the hobbies and the energy, feeling down still feels like it requires some kind of emotional weight, you know? Like, if you're depressed, I imagine you feel heavy or sad or you cry, or you have these dark thoughts circling in your head. But I don't have any of that. It's just... blank. It's not a heavy feeling, it's just an empty feeling. \n\nI actually remember my mom asking me something similar, maybe a year ago? It was winter, I know because I was wearing this thick gray sweater she bought me, the one with the big buttons down the front, and I was just sitting on my bed staring at the corner of the room where the paint is peeling a little bit. And she came in and sat next to me and she was crying, and she asked, \"Are you so sad, honey? Are you just so depressed you can't move?\" And I remember looking at her and trying to find some sadness in myself to match hers, because she was so upset, but there was just nothing there. I didn't feel like crying. I didn't feel sorrow. I didn't feel anything at all. \n\nSo I told her no, I'm not sad. And I think that almost confused her more. Because people expect that if you're not doing anything, if you're just existing in your room for two years, you must be drowning in this deep, dark depression. But I'm not drowning. It's more like... the water just evaporated. There's no water to drown in. There's no sadness, no feeling down. Just the flat line. So, no, I haven't had times where I felt depressed most of the day, because I don't really feel much of anything most of the day.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when, aside from the flatness, you felt so depressed or down that it seriously interfered with your ability to function?\n\nPatient: Um, no, I haven't. I mean, I know you just asked about feeling depressed or down, and I guess this is kind of the same thing, but for two weeks? No. Not even for two weeks. Like I was saying, there's just no water to drown in. It's not like I have this baseline of being flat and then suddenly, for a couple of weeks, I dip down into this really dark, heavy depression where I can't function because I'm so sad. \n\nMy functioning is already... well, it's already what it is. I sit in my room. I look at the carpet. But it's not because I'm overwhelmed by sadness or despair. It's just the emptiness. I don't have these episodes where the flatness suddenly turns into some intense, agonizing depression that stops me from doing things. The flatness is what stops me from doing things. \n\nI remember reading once, back when I used to read things for that English class I never finished, about how depression can make people feel like they're walking through molasses, you know? Like everything is thick and heavy and takes so much effort just to push through. But for me, it's not like walking through molasses. It's like... not walking at all. It's like the concept of walking just doesn't even apply anymore. There's no struggle against a heavy feeling, there's just an absence of the drive to move. \n\nSo, no, I haven't had any two-week periods where I felt so depressed it interfered with my functioning. My functioning has been exactly the same—just sitting there, staring at the floor, listening to the hum of the refrigerator from the kitchen—every day for the last two years and two months. There hasn't been any dip into sadness or anything like that. Just the same flat line, day after day, week after week.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any period of at least two weeks when you felt clearly depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Um, no. I mean, I know you're asking about the two weeks thing again, but it's really just exactly like I was saying before. There hasn't been a time where I felt depressed or down like that. Not for two weeks, not for two days. It's just... I think people really struggle to understand that you can be completely non-functional without being sad. \n\nLike, my mom, she's always trying to find a reason for it. She'll come into my room and she'll open the curtains, the ones with the little blue flowers on them that we picked out when I was in middle school, and she'll say, \"Let some light in, maybe it'll lift your mood.\" And the light comes in, and it hits the carpet, and I can see all the little dust motes floating in the sunbeam, just drifting around in the air. I can watch them for hours, just seeing how they catch the light and then disappear into the shadows near the closet door. But watching them doesn't make me feel better, and it doesn't make me feel worse. It just... is. \n\nI don't have a mood to lift. That's the thing. If I was depressed, like really down and sad for two weeks, maybe the sunlight would hurt my eyes, or maybe I'd want to hide under the covers and cry because the world is too bright and I'm too sad. But I don't do that. I just sit there on the edge of the bed and look at the dust motes. I don't feel the urge to cry, I don't feel a heaviness in my chest. I just feel the complete absence of anything. \n\nSo, no, there's never been a two-week period of feeling clearly depressed or down. It's always just the flat line. Sometimes she makes those little frozen pizza rolls, or sometimes it's just a turkey sandwich, and she actually cuts the crusts off now, which she hasn't done since I was maybe seven years old. I think she does it because she thinks I'm fragile now, or maybe she just wants to feel like she's doing something special to take care of me since I don't leave the room. \n\nBut I eat it. I don't look at the tray and feel sick, or think, \"Oh, I can't possibly eat.\" I just take the plate, and I sit on the edge of the bed, and I chew. I'll take a bite of the sandwich, and I'll chew it, and I'll swallow it, and then I'll take a sip of water from the blue plastic cup she always brings. It's just mechanics, you know? Like putting gas in a car that's just sitting in the driveway and never going anywhere. \n\nSometimes I'll sit there for an hour, just holding a piece of bread, looking at the way the crust is slightly darker on one side, feeling the soft texture of it between my fingers before I take the next bite. I can feel the crumbs falling onto the blanket. But I always finish it. It doesn't really taste like much anymore—not good, not bad, just texture and chewing. But my stomach still growls if she's late bringing the tray. Like, if she goes to the grocery store and lunch is at two instead of noon, my stomach makes noises. I just eat the food she brings in the exact same flat way I do everything else. No. I haven't ever had two weeks like that. \n\nIt's strange, though, how time works when you're just... sitting. Um, dead? No. I don't... I don't think about that. Hurting myself... no. 

There is this pair of scissors on the desk in the corner of my room. They have these bright orange plastic handles, the kind they used to give us in middle school art class. I mean... I don't really think it's changed. It's just about the same, I guess. I haven't really noticed it being any different, mostly because I'm just in the room all the time anyway.

I mean... I think I kind of already told you that, didn't I? About how I haven't had a time like this before? Because, like I was saying, there wasn't any other period where things were different from how they usually were. 

My baseline... if that's what you want to call it... was just doing the exact same things every single day. There were no interruptions. Like, after school, the bus would drop me off at the corner, right next to this big, dark green metal mail relay box. Someone had spray-painted the letters 'J.K.' on the side of it in this really bright neon pink, but the paint was chipping off in these tiny little flakes, especially around the edges of the 'K', because of the rain and the weather. I would walk past that green box every single afternoon at exactly 3:15. 

And from that box to the edge of my driveway, there were exactly 47 squares of concrete on the sidewalk. I know because I counted them every time I walked home. The 23rd square had this deep crack right across the middle that looked exactly like a sideways letter 'Y', and in the spring, this one single dandelion would grow right out of the very center of the crack. Just one, never two. I would just step right over it, carrying that same blue backpack with the broken zipper I told you about, and I would go inside and sit at the kitchen table.

The bottom left corner of the paper is curled up into a little tube because the door brushes against the carpet whenever it opens, which isn't very often. I never flipped the page to February. It's just been stuck on January for two whole years. \n\nI look at that gray rock a lot. I've counted the pine trees. There are forty-seven of them, if you include the ones that are cut off by the edge of the glossy paper. And over the past two years, while that calendar has just been hanging there getting older, I've just been sitting here. That has happened over seven hundred times since that calendar was supposed to be used. \n\nAnd during all those days, I haven't felt low. I haven't felt depressed. Two weeks sounds like a really specific, long amount of time when you say it like that, but for me, two weeks is just fourteen days of watching the ceiling fan. We have this ceiling fan in my bedroom, it has four blades, and one of them is slightly warped. It droops down just a fraction of an inch more than the other three. The blades are wood-paneled on one side and plain white on the other, and my dad installed it white-side down when I was ten because he said it made the ceiling look higher. \n\nI just lie on the bed and watch it not spinning. I can trace the dust along the edge of the warped blade with my eyes. Sometimes I think about what it would feel like to actually care that it's warped, or to feel sad that fourteen days—or a whole month, or a year—are just slipping by while I look at it. If I were actually depressed, like really down the way you keep asking about, maybe I'd cry about wasting my time or something. People who are depressed feel heavy and miserable about things like that, right? They feel bad about themselves. But I don't feel miserable. I don't feel anything about the fan, or the two weeks, or the fact that it's been over a year since high school ended and I'm just here in this room. \n\nSo, yeah, no. I haven't been depressed or down for two weeks. There's no sadness to it. It's just the flat. Just the warped fan blade, and the quiet, and the flat.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling worthless or like a failure?\n\nPatient: Um, worthless? Or a failure? No... I don't think so. I mean, to feel like a failure, you have to actually have a goal that you care about failing at, right? You have to feel some kind of disappointment in yourself, or care about what you're supposed to be doing. But I don't have that. \n\nLike, my high school diploma is sitting on the third shelf of my bookcase, the one right next to the window. It's in this dark green padded folder with the school crest stamped on it in gold foil, and the gold is actually starting to flake off just a tiny bit on the left edge of the shield. I can see the little specks of gold dust on the wood of the shelf if the light hits it right. Sometimes my mom comes in to take my empty plates, and I see her look at that green folder, and then she looks at me just sitting on the bed. I know she's probably thinking about how I was supposed to be finishing that community college program by now. I just stopped going, you know. I didn't make a big decision to quit, I just stopped getting up to go. \n\nBut when I look at the diploma, or when I think about the college classes I'm not taking, my chest doesn't get tight. I don't feel ashamed. I don't sit here thinking, \"Oh, I'm so worthless, I'm a failure because I'm nineteen and I just watch the ceiling fan all day.\" I just look at the green folder. I look at the little flakes of gold on the wood. I don't feel bad about myself, and I don't feel good about myself either. \n\nI think a failure would be upset about failing. They would cry, or feel guilty that their mom is bringing them turkey sandwiches with the crusts cut off while they do absolutely nothing. But I don't feel guilty. It's just like the dust motes and the warped fan blade. I just exist in the room. There's no judgment attached to it in my head. I'm not worth less, I'm not worth more. I'm just... here. So, no, I haven't been feeling worthless.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any thoughts that you would be better off dead or thoughts of hurting yourself?\n\nPatient: Um, dead? No. I don't... I don't think about that. Hurting myself... no. \n\nThere is this pair of scissors on the desk in the corner of my room. They have these bright orange plastic handles, the kind they used to give us in middle school art class. The metal is a little dull on one side, and there is a tiny spot of dried white glue near the hinge from when I tried to fix a broken picture frame maybe three years ago. Sometimes the light from the streetlamp outside catches the metal at night, and it just shines there in the dark. I know people who are really sad, people who want to die, they might look at something sharp like that and think about using it to stop feeling so bad. They want the pain to end. But I don't have any pain to end. I just look at the scissors and think about how the orange plastic is slightly faded on the left grip. I don't want to pick them up. I don't want to hurt myself. \n\nI don't want to die, either. Dying seems like it would take a lot of effort, actually. You have to actively want something to change to want to be dead, I think. You have to be running away from something terrible. But I am not running. I am just sitting here. Breathing in and out. The air in my room always smells a little bit like the lavender laundry detergent my mom uses because she washes the curtains every single month, trying to keep the dust down since I am in here all the time. I just breathe it in. I don't wish I would stop breathing. It is just an automatic thing my body does, like my stomach growling when lunch is late. \n\nSo, no, I haven't had any thoughts about being better off dead or hurting myself. I don't really have thoughts about being better off at all. I am just existing. It is just neutral.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt clearly depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Um... you're asking me that again. The two weeks thing. I'm pretty sure we started with that exact question, didn't we? About feeling clearly depressed or down nearly every day. I was just looking at it. So, even if you ask me a third time, or a fourth time, it's just going to be the same answer. Just no.\n\nDoctor: Over the past two years, have you ever had a depressed or low mood most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: I mean... now you're just stretching the time out. First it was two weeks, now it's two years. But changing the number of days doesn't change what I'm telling you. It's still no. The picture has this huge, sheer gray rock face, and at the very bottom, there are these dark green pine trees with tiny patches of white snow on the branches.
